newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian parties clash on new election law.
newsitem.headline: Albanian parties clash on new election law.

text.p: Albania's political parties clashed over a new election law on Tuesday as Western security officials worked to prevent a fresh crisis and keep promised elections on track for the end of June.

The elections are a key element of international efforts to prevent Albania sliding once more into the chaos and violence of February and March after the collapse of high-yielding pyramid investment schemes.
Under a six-point political contract brokered by OSCE envoy Franz Vranitzky last week, the election law should have been passed on Monday but that deadline has already been missed.
A fresh row broke out on Tuesday as the Socialists accused the former ruling Democratic Party of President Sali Berisha of trying to railroad its own election bill through parliament.
Western diplomats said there was a danger that if the Democrats force through their own law then other parties would refuse to take part in elections, leading to more chaos.
Socialist deputy parliament speaker Hamit Gjoni said the Democrats' move could cause a fresh government crisis.
"We are categorically against the introduction of this law because we have the draft law prepared by the nine-party government," he told parliament.
"The introduction of a different draft creates the basis for a government crisis and the destabilisation of the country," he said.
Under the Vranitzky contract, parliament must pass the law so Berisha can call a poll by May 15. Albanian law says the president has to call elections at least 45 days before voting.

The Socialists said an election law presented by the Democratic Party conflicted with the Vranitzky deal as it was not approved by the nine-party Government of National Reconciliation, formed amid the rioting in March.
The Socialists also objected to the proposed division of seats to be decided by proportional and majority voting.
They said the only election law they would debate was one presented by the government.
"I am trying to resist in this game (against the Democrats) but I am very much available for a compromise," Fatos Nano, leader of the Socialist Party, told Reuters.
As the politicians argued, officials of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), brokering the talks, were busy trying to find a compromise.
One Western security official said there was disappointment that the Democratic Party had drafted its own law and that intensive talks were being held to clarify the situation.
The Socialists want more seats to be decided by a proportional vote to allow smaller parties a voice in parliament and lead to the formation of a coalition government.
The Democrats want more seats on a majority system, as in the 1996 elections when they won 122 of 140 seats.
International observers said that poll was flawed and it was boycotted by the Socialists on the last day.
But the Democratic Party said its draft law was in line with the Vranitzky deal.

"It is indispensable the procedure be quickened if we want to respect the political contract. Today is the deadline if elections have to take place in the required date," said Ali Spahia, chairman of the Democratic Party parliamentary group.
Under the proposed new Democrats' law, 115 seats would be decided by a majority vote and 40 by a proportional system.
The Socialists said they were also opposed to that formula.
Another key point of the Vranitzky contract was the disbanding of so-called salvation committees in the south of the country by May 14.
They were set up to restore some kind of order after riots and are only due to meet on May 16.
